candidateRows: Important notions of freedom and willing can survive determinism without preserving libertarian alternative possibilities or ultimate sourcehood.
This states the compatibilist side's governing thesis and reframes the dispute around forms of agency that remain meaningful under determinism.

After distinguishing libertarianism and incompatibilist denial, Joe presents his own unorthodox compatibilism as an inquiry into freedom and will that remain intact regardless of the underlying metaphysics.
Libertarian freedom best fits the experienced structure of deliberation, control, selection among genuine options, and action.
This supplies the libertarian side's principal positive case by grounding alternative possibilities and agency in ordinary deliberative experience.

Nathan accepts the basic taxonomy, describes conscious consideration and selection among options, argues that libertarianism captures this experience, and distinguishes causal from non-causal determinism.
Determinative relations need not be causal, because logical or mathematical entailment can fix an outcome without pushing, forcing, or temporally producing it.
The causal versus non-causal distinction structures later disagreement about whether determination threatens agency through restraint or merely entails facts.
Nathan explains determination through relations between facts, uses mathematical entailment as the model of a non-causal relation, and contrasts it with temporally sequenced forcing or restraint.
Scientific presentations of free will as a settled impossibility often rely on interpretive assumptions and understate unresolved issues involving causation and time.
This challenges a major route to denying freedom by denying that current science has resolved the philosophical dependencies of the free-will question.
Popular scientific arguments claiming that empirical research has already established that human beings lack free will.
Asked why people deny free will, Nathan contrasts the complexity of specialist work on freedom, causation, and time with simplified popular treatments and argues that the matter remains open.
Deliberation is a directed process integrating imagined options, rational and emotional evaluation, and control systems rather than thoughts merely appearing without agency.
This directly defends the phenomenology and proposed neural architecture of libertarian deliberation against introspective and neuroscientific objections.
Sam Harris's claim that thoughts simply arise and that brain activity predicts decisions before conscious choice occurs.
Nathan describes goal-directed evaluation of imagined alternatives and invokes a neuroscientific account involving valitional, imaginative, and emotional systems to resist a passive model of thought.
Neuroscientific findings about decision-making should receive limited philosophical weight because the field and its indirect measurement methods remain comparatively immature.
This limits the force of empirical arguments used by either side and establishes Joe's methodological basis for withholding strong conclusions from disputed experiments.
The preceding appeal to neuroscience as either undermining or vindicating conscious free choice.

Joe treats the relevant experiments cautiously, notes that common imaging measures are removed from neural activity, emphasizes the field's youth, and defers to methodological criticism by specialists.
Non-causal determinism is more credible than causal determinism and is obscured when popular discussion treats all determination as a causal sequence.
The claim identifies the form of determinism Joe favors and separates foreknowledge or entailment from causal production, shaping his compatibilist account.
Joe argues that popular treatments collapse two distinct relations, uses complete knowledge of successive facts and divine foreknowledge as non-causal models, and states his comparative commitment.
Under physicalism or monism, an antecedent brain state is part of the acting person, so neural prediction does not by itself displace personal agency.
This neutralizes the inference from neural antecedence to non-agency by denying the separation between the person and the person's physical realization.
The inference that a prior neural event, rather than the person, produces an action and therefore eliminates personal agency.

Joe argues that separating a person's action from the person's brain imports a dualistic picture inconsistent with monism, and adds that predictability from brains or past behavior need not be threatening.
Even in a deterministic world, practically important distinctions between willing and unwilling action, including consent, remain available and support compatibilist agency.
This gives a concrete foundation for compatibilism by identifying normatively and practically indispensable forms of will that survive determination.
Joe asks what distinctions people would still need under determinism, emphasizes willing action and consent, and argues that non-causal determination avoids the image of an external puppeteer.
Indeterminism is not equivalent to randomness, because constrained probabilistic variation can permit choices whose lack of a further physical explanation does not make them reasonless.
This answers a central hard-incompatibilist dilemma by defending a conceptual space for libertarian selection between determination and mere randomness.
The hard-incompatibilist objection that every event is either determined or random and that neither possibility permits free will.

Nathan rejects the proposed dichotomy, distinguishes absence of determination from chaos, describes probabilistic variation within constraints, and argues that a choice can be physically brute without being merely random.
Weighted stochastic decision processes may still fail to provide the unrestricted authorship that incompatibilists associate with libertarian freedom.
The move directly tests whether Hawkins's indeterministic, criteria-weighted neuroscience escapes randomness and supplies the alternative possibilities demanded by the motion.
Hawkins's claim that criteria-weighted indeterminacy avoids the simple determined-or-random dilemma.

Folley develops possible incompatibilist objections: weighted probabilities may remain randomness-like, inherited criteria undermine sourcehood, and replayed choices may lack unrestricted alternatives.
If the self is identified with the brain's valitional executive system, then the self participates in setting the criteria that guide indeterminate choices.
This answer addresses the sourcehood objection by locating personal agency within the neural system that constrains and evaluates genuinely open possibilities.
Folley's suggestion that probabilistic weighting does not show that the person genuinely authors the resulting choice.
Hawkins argues that critics either deny a self or identify it with some brain system; on the latter view, the relevant executive system sets the decision criteria.
Rejecting a self-causing, quasi-dualist will does not eliminate the practical notions of responsibility, choice, consent, and agency that compatibilists seek to preserve.
The move states the compatibilist core of the debate: even if an especially demanding conception of libertarian will fails, substantial practical agency can survive.
Hawkins's contention that identifying the self with executive neural functions supplies the agency incompatibilists demand.

Folley explains why hard incompatibilists may treat freedom as requiring a self-causing entity, then argues that little follows from rejecting that picture because many practical concepts remain recoverable.
Both agent causation and criterial neural causation offer conceptually coherent ways for the person to originate an action without a prior sufficient physical cause.
The move supplies positive models of libertarian sourcehood, directly answering the demand for an originating agent rather than merely undetermined neural activity.
Folley's claim that hard incompatibilists are targeting a self-causing will whose loss leaves practical agency largely intact.
Hawkins outlines Chisholm-style agent causation, then argues that if the person is a valitional brain system, criterial causation already makes that system causally relevant to action.
Because genetics and upbringing heavily shape the criteria governing choice, a criterial-causation model may not provide the ultimate sourcehood libertarianism requires.
The objection targets the origin of the agent's evaluative standards, challenging whether indeterminism at the point of decision is enough for libertarian responsibility.
Hawkins's proposal that the valitional brain system supplies the relevant source of criterial constraints and subsequent action.
Folley grants that later adjustment may occur but argues that many constraints on the criteria and available possibilities arise from factors outside the agent's control.
Libertarian freedom can operate within inherited limits because agents contribute to self-realization through choices that reshape their future dispositions and possibilities.
The response defends meaningful agency without requiring freedom from every biological or social influence, and explains how small choices can alter later capacities.
Folley's objection that genetics, upbringing, and other uncontrolled factors determine the criteria that constrain possible choices.
Hawkins accepts substantial biological and social influence but argues that agents play the hand they receive, with repeated decisions changing their brains, abilities, and future option sets.
The phenomenology of deliberation and choice should be taken seriously, and an idealist monism naturally expects it to have a corresponding neural manifestation.
The move supplies an independent epistemic and metaphysical basis for libertarian agency rather than relying exclusively on a contested neuroscientific mechanism.
Folley's question whether Hawkins's libertarian view rests on other commitments or mainly on an intuition drawn from deliberative experience.
Hawkins presents an inside-out idealist explanation: physical reality expresses mental reality, so subjective choosing should possess a physical correlate visible in brain activity.
Hawkins's limited libertarianism cannot guarantee ultimate responsibility for agents whose evaluative criteria were formed within severely constraining environments.
The example tests whether Hawkins's account delivers the sourcehood and responsibility commonly expected of libertarian freedom when character formation is externally constrained.
Hawkins's bounded libertarian account in which agents contribute to self-realization despite biological and social constraints.

Folley uses an agent raised entirely in a racist community to argue that constrained criteria may block responsibility, while noting that Hawkins's modest view differs from popular libertarian expectations.
Compatibilism should reconstruct the practically important distinctions between willed and unwilled action that remain available under determinism.
This is a direct positive defense of the motion's compatibilist alternative, grounding responsibility-relevant agency in distinctions that survive deterministic explanation.
Folley distinguishes reflexes from choices, then uses two deterministic agents—one affected by a removable brain tumor—to show why predictive and responsibility-relevant distinctions remain useful.
Undetermined neural firing combined with system-level criterial causation supplies both open alternatives and top-down control rather than mere event-level randomness.
The response connects indeterminacy to agent-level control, addressing the central objection that libertarian alternatives are either causally determined or merely random.
Folley's challenges concerning an uncaused neuron and whether Hawkins's criterial model provides the control expected from libertarianism.
Hawkins argues that synaptic indeterminacy leaves some neural firing without a sufficient cause while system-level criterial causation imposes top-down constraints of a different causal kind.
A libertarian appeal to live options needs a principled account of when alternatives are genuinely available, especially because ordinary responsibility judgments persist in constrained cases.
The move challenges the operational boundary of the pro side's central condition for freedom and uses responsibility data to pressure its explanatory adequacy.
Hawkins's claim that responsibility depends on having genuine live alternative possibilities.

After Hawkins limits libertarian freedom to live options, Folley questions how those options can be identified and argues that judgments about Jojo suggest responsibility survives severe formative constraint.
Libertarian freedom includes alternative possibilities and sourcehood, while moral responsibility primarily concerns the person's accumulated role in shaping their own character.
This move directly states the pro side's conception of libertarian freedom and connects it to a substantive theory of responsibility grounded in character formation.
Folley's objection that constrained agents like Jojo remain commonly judged responsible despite lacking clear live options.
Hawkins answers that people struggle to imagine an agent with no opportunity to resist, then shifts from isolated choices to the cumulative decisions through which a person shapes character.
Determinism can preserve responsibility through causal feedback, proximal agency, and character-based prediction even when an agent could not have acted otherwise.
The move supplies a direct compatibilist reconstruction of the pro side's character-formation account, denying that alternative possibilities are required for agency or responsibility.
Hawkins's claim that accumulated self-shaping choices ground responsibility within a libertarian framework.
Folley argues that upbringing and genetics can deterministically initiate a person while later feedback processes still make character predictively and causally relevant to future conduct.
Freedom and responsibility form a plural family of concepts whose practical role in praise and blame should guide theory rather than a single metaphysical definition.
This reframes the debate away from necessary and sufficient metaphysical conditions and toward the practical functions of freedom and responsibility judgments.
The libertarian attempt to make alternative possibilities and self-formation jointly determine responsibility judgments.
Folley contrasts deterministic responsibility with libertarian unfreedom under coercion, surveys several compatibilist models, and proposes starting from reactive attitudes and their practical uses.
A pragmatist who takes deliberative phenomenology and causal reasoning seriously should affirm subjective sourcehood and the truth of alternative possibilities.
The move turns the con side's pragmatic methodology into a direct argument for the pro side's defining claims of ultimate sourcehood and the ability to do otherwise.
Folley's pragmatic proposal to begin with the functions of freedom and responsibility ascriptions rather than metaphysical freedom.
Hawkins argues that agents experience deliberation as originating causal chains and that pragmatism should validate this useful, responsibility-guiding practice, including its alternatives.
The ineliminable first-person experience of deliberating as able to do otherwise creates a serious unresolved challenge for a deterministic compatibilist view.
This is a substantial concession that the pro side's phenomenological argument pressures determinism at least for self-understanding, while stopping short of full libertarian endorsement.
Hawkins's argument that pragmatic validation of deliberative phenomenology supports sourcehood and genuine alternatives.
Folley says he may adopt deterministic attitudes toward others but cannot clearly do so toward himself while deliberating, leaving the first-person case unresolved within his theory.
Because evolved deliberation and inquiry are practically effective, pragmatism should treat their embedded conception of agency and alternative possibilities as true.
The move reinforces the prior phenomenological argument with an evolutionary and epistemic basis, contending that the con side's own pragmatism validates libertarian-seeming agency.
Folley's uncertainty over whether first-person deliberative experience can be reconciled with his deterministic commitments.
Hawkins argues that deliberative consciousness was retained because it works and that inquiry itself depends on considering possibilities, so pragmatism cannot dismiss its alternative structure.
Folley cannot consistently reserve source-like agency for himself because his interpretations of others already distinguish genuine agents from merely compelled behavior.
The move attacks the coherence of restricting first-person sourcehood by arguing that interpersonal reactive attitudes already presuppose a comparable distinction in others.
Folley's proposal that first-person deliberation may be exceptional while other agents can still be understood compatibilistically.
Hawkins invokes ordinary differences between intentional conduct, being shoved, and behavior caused by a brain tumor to argue that Folley treats other people as genuine agents too.
A proximal-source account can distinguish choices from nonchoices under determinism without requiring the ability to do otherwise or weakening agency under decisive reasons.
This is the con side's clearest compact statement that practical agency can survive determinism through sourcehood short of libertarian ultimacy and without alternate possibilities.
Hawkins's claim that Folley's treatment of other agents implicitly commits him to sourcehood and alternative possibilities.
Folley says even conclusive proof of determinism would leave meaningful distinctions between choices and nonchoices intact, and that overwhelming reasons do not make decisions less agential.
The tension between first-person inquiry and scientific self-description is a deep, near-universal problem rather than a distinctive failure of pragmatic compatibilism.
The move limits the force of Hawkins's objection by relocating it within a broader epistemic problem faced by any view that studies humans as both inquirers and objects.
Hawkins's attempt to use the unavoidable first-person standpoint as a special argument for libertarian freedom.
Folley explains that humans both measure the world and become objects of empirical measurement, making it difficult to reconcile deliberative subjectivity with naturalistic self-study on any theory.
